result:
The morning light hit the windowsill differently that Tuesday, and I noticed because I'd stopped noticing for three years. That's how it works, isn't it? The things you see every day become invisible until something cracks, and then you see everything. The dust. The way the paint peels exactly where your thumb rests when you close the cabinet. The neighbor's dog that barks at 6:47, not 6:45, and you've been wrong about it for months.

I used to collect rocks as a child. Not interesting rocks—just rocks. Gray ones from the driveway, reddish ones from the elementary school playground, a white one I convinced myself was a fossil because it had a stripe. My mother threw them out during a move, and I cried for an hour, which seems excessive now, but I was mourning something I couldn't name. The weight of them in my pockets. The way they grounded me when the world felt too fast, too loud, too full of people expecting me to be someone I hadn't figured out how to be yet.

My grandmother spoke to her plants. Not in a whimsical way, not "grow big and strong" nonsense. She told them about her day. "Mrs. Henderson asked me to make three pies for the church auction and I said yes because I can't say no, and now my hands hurt already thinking about it." The plants never answered, which was perhaps the point. She died with a fern on her hospital nightstand, and I wondered later if anyone thought to water it, if it died too, if someone threw it out with the get-well balloons.

I've been thinking about inheritance. Not money. The other things. The way my father clears his throat before he says something difficult, which I do now. The recipe for potato soup that isn't written anywhere but lives in my hands, muscle memory of how much milk, when the potatoes are soft enough. The fear of open water. The particular angle of my mother's handwriting, which I copied so obsessively in sixth grade that now mine is indistinguishable from hers, and sometimes I can't remember which of us wrote a note.

Time is a liar. It tells you that the difficult thing you're doing is permanent, that you'll always feel this tired, this uncertain, this quietly desperate in grocery store parking lots. Then it tells you that the good thing was fleeting, that you should have paid better attention, that you'll never feel that particular joy again. Both are true and neither are true, and the trick is holding both without letting them crush you flat.

I met a man once who'd walked across Spain. The Camino, though he didn't call it that, just "the walk." He said the hardest part was the flat stretches, not the mountains. "Your mind needs the struggle," he told me, drinking coffee I hadn't asked to buy him. "When it's easy, you remember why you're walking, and sometimes that's worse than blisters." I thought he was being dramatic, the way people are about things they've done that they need to matter. But I remember it now, the flat stretches, the days when nothing happens and that's somehow unbearable.

We don't talk enough about maintenance. The work of keeping things going. Marriage, yes, but also: the furnace filter, the friendship you have to keep choosing, the body that needs more sleep than you want to give it, the creative practice that feels pointless on the bad days. Everyone celebrates starting. The new job, the first date, the blank page. No one throws a party for the third year of something, the ordinary Tuesday when you do it again because you said you would, and saying you would matters even when the doing feels small.

I read once that the human brain can't distinguish between physical and social pain, that rejection activates the same regions as a broken arm. I don't know if that's true, but I know that some goodbyes still ache in my body years later, specific locations I could point to. The stomach, mostly. The chest. The place behind my eyes that hurts when I'm trying not to cry in public, which happens more than I'd like to admit, because I cry at commercials, at old people holding hands, at the particular slant of autumn light through yellow leaves that means something is ending and I don't know how to hold the beauty and the grief together.

The last time I saw my childhood home, someone else lived there. They'd painted the door red, which looked wrong, though I couldn't say why. The tree I'd climbed was gone, not even a stump. I stood in the street for too long, and a woman came out and asked if I needed help, and I couldn't explain that I was haunting my own life, that I was a ghost in a place that had stopped being mine without asking permission. She looked concerned. I left. I think about that door sometimes, how red it was, how final.

There's a theory I like, probably unscientific, that we leave pieces of ourselves in places we've been, that a version of you still exists in every room you ever loved, every car that carried you somewhere important, every corner of the world where you were changed. I hope that's true. I hope there's a version of me still in my grandmother's kitchen, learning to roll pie crust, still in the passenger seat of my best friend's car at seventeen, singing too loud with the windows down, still on a beach in Oregon watching my dog run in circles because the sand was new and everything was possible. I hope they're happy, those versions. I hope they know I'm still here, carrying them, trying to be worth what they believed.

I'm running out of words, and I haven't said anything important, not really. But maybe that's the point. The unimportant things are what stay. The way your coffee tastes on a normal morning. The specific sound of someone you love coming home. The rocks in your pocket, heavy and real, grounding you in a world that keeps spinning, indifferent and beautiful, terrible and brief, yours while you have it, which is never long enough, which is always, somehow, exactly long enough.
